subject: Physics
topic: Why metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature
title: Why Metal Feels Colder than Wood
summary: A steel railing and a wooden bench at the same 10 °C, yet the steel feels icy. Skin senses how fast heat leaves it, and metal conducts heat hundreds of times faster than wood.

notes.title: 02 – Why Metal Feels Colder than Wood

keyPoints: Objects left together reach the **same temperature** (a thermometer reads both 10 °C).
Skin does not sense temperature directly; it senses the **rate of heat flow** out of (or into) it.
Metal is a good **conductor**: it pulls heat from your finger and spreads it away, so the skin cools fast.
Wood is an **insulator**: heat leaves slowly and the touched spot warms up, so it does not feel cold. On a hot day metal feels hotter for the same reason.

list: Cooking pans are metal (heat flows in fast); handles are wood or plastic (heat flows slowly).
A tiled floor feels colder than a carpet in the same room.
A metal seat in the sun can burn, while a wooden bench beside it is only warm.

simulation.reason: Changing the material and the temperature and watching two fingers on two surfaces lets students test the idea themselves: the objects share one temperature, yet heat leaves the skin at different rates, and above skin temperature the feel reverses.
simulation.objective: See why two objects at the same temperature feel different, and how the feel reverses above skin temperature.
instructions: Choose a material for each hand.
Set the temperature of both objects with the slider.
Press Touch both, or drag the time slider, and watch the contact temperature and heat flow.
Raise the temperature above 33 °C and see the feel reverse.
